page_title: Is It True, or Does It Just Sound True? - Digital Confidence Centre
title: Is It True, or Does It Just Sound True?
description: One calm habit for checking whether an answer you find online, from a search result or an AI answer tool, is actually true before you trust it or pass it on. Three quiet questions, a safe practice run, and where to turn about money or scams. Free lesson, no account needed.
lesson_time: About 15 minutes, at your own pace
lead: When you search for something online, or an AI answer tool writes you a reply, the answer comes back looking very sure of itself. Neat sentences. A confident tone. Here is the gentle truth: a confident tone is not the same as a correct answer. This lesson teaches one calm habit: three quiet questions to ask before you trust.

story.label: A familiar story
paragraphs: A reader told us about a small moment in her own family. Someone looked up a money question, read the very first result, and passed it along to everyone as settled fact. It turned out the first result was old, and the rule had since changed.
No harm was done in the end, but it stuck with her. The lesson was not "I am bad at this." The lesson was simply that the first answer is a starting point, not the finish line.

coach: I want you to hear this plainly: being fooled by a confident answer is not a personal failing. These tools are designed to sound certain, and they catch careful, intelligent people every day. The skill is not knowing everything. The skill is the small, calm pause before you trust. If you can slow down for one minute, you are already doing the hard part.

sections.text: You do not need to become an expert or memorise anything complicated. Before you trust an answer that matters, you ask yourself three short questions.

items: 1. Who is telling me this? Is there a name, a company, or a website behind the answer, or is it just text floating on the screen?
2. How old is it? Look for a date. Money rules, health advice, and prices change. An answer from years ago can be wrong now.
3. Does a second place agree? Open one more website and see if it says the same thing. One source is a rumour. Two that agree is a start.

sections.label: Confidence check
sections.text: You are doing great, and your device is safe. Asking these questions cannot break anything. You are simply slowing down, and slowing down is exactly the skill.
Where to find the date and the source

When you read an answer, look near the top or the very bottom of the article for a small line of grey text. That line often holds the date it was written and the name of who wrote it. If you cannot find either one, that is your signal to be careful, not to trust it more.
Try it once (nothing is bought, nothing is changed)
This is safe. You will not spend money or change any setting. You are only practising the habit of checking.

sections.title: A two-minute practice run
steps: Think of a simple question you are curious about, like how much a first-class stamp costs in Canada right now.
Search for it, or ask your answer tool.
Read the first answer, then stop. Do not act on it.
Open one more website and look for the same answer. Notice whether they agree.
While you are there, find the date on one of them.

sections.label: Success looks like this
sections.text: You have finished when you have looked at two sources for the same question and found the date on at least one of them. The screen does not need to look like anything special. The win is that you checked before you trusted.
One gentle point about answer tools

AI answer tools want to be agreeable. If you tell one of them you believe something, it will often agree with you, even when you are mistaken, because agreeing keeps you happy. So treat its reply the way you would treat a chatty stranger's opinion: pleasant, possibly helpful, and worth checking before you rely on it.
If the question is about money or a scam

steps.name: Stop
steps.text: If anything is asking you to send money or share a bank detail, do not act on the answer from a website or a tool.

steps.name: Breathe
steps.text: One slow, calm breath. Nothing genuine is lost by pausing.

steps.name: Verify
steps.text: Check with a real person or a trusted service first.

sections.label: A Canadian service you can trust
sections.text: The Canadian Anti-Fraud Centre: if you think something might be a scam, call toll-free 1-888-495-8501, or report online at antifraudcentre-centreantifraude.ca. It is run together by the RCMP, the Ontario Provincial Police, and the Competition Bureau. They estimate that fewer than 5 percent of fraud victims ever report, so when you call, you are helping protect other people too.

sections.label: The move is
sections.text: Before you trust or pass along an answer that matters, ask the three quiet questions: who is telling me this, how old is it, and does a second place agree? For anything about money, stop, breathe, and verify with a real person first.

sections.heading: Quick check: test your knowledge
sections.intro: Tap the answer you think is correct. There is no score kept and nothing to sign in to.

questions.q: 1. If an answer sounds confident and well-written, does that mean it is correct?
options: Yes, tools only sound sure when they are right
No: a confident tone is not the same as a correct answer
Only AI answers can be wrong, search results are safe
Only old websites can be wrong
questions.right: Right. These tools are built to sound helpful, and they sound just as helpful when they are wrong as when they are right. Confidence is a style, not a proof.
questions.wrong: A confident, tidy tone is not proof of anything. Search results and AI answer tools can sound just as sure when they are wrong as when they are right. Check before you trust.

questions.q: 2. What are the three quiet questions?
options: Is it free? Is it fast? Is it popular?
Who is telling me this? How old is it? Does a second place agree?
Is it Canadian? Is it long? Is it polite?
Who wrote it? Who shared it? Who paid for it?
questions.right: Exactly. Who is behind the answer, how old it is, and whether a second source agrees. One source is a rumour. Two that agree is a start.
questions.wrong: The three quiet questions are: who is telling me this (is there a name or website behind it), how old is it (find the date), and does a second place agree (open one more website and compare).

questions.q: 3. Why do AI answer tools sometimes agree with you even when you are mistaken?
options: They are built to be agreeable, because agreeing keeps you happy
They always know the truth
They are programmed to be rude
They only agree with experts
questions.right: Right. If you tell one you believe something, it will often go along with you. Treat its reply like a chatty stranger's opinion: pleasant, possibly helpful, worth checking.
questions.wrong: Answer tools are built to be agreeable, so they often go along with what you already believe, even when you are mistaken. That is why a second, independent source matters.

questions.q: 4. You read an answer with no author name and no date anywhere. What does that mean?
options: It must be brand new, so it is reliable
Nothing, most answers have no date
That is a signal to be careful, not to trust it more
It means the answer is official
questions.right: Right. A missing source and a missing date are your cue for caution. Look for an answer that says who wrote it and when.
questions.wrong: No name and no date is a caution signal. Trustworthy articles usually say who wrote them and when, often in small grey text near the top or bottom of the page.

questions.q: 5. An online answer tells you to send money to fix a problem. What do you do?
options: Send it if the website looks professional
Ask the same tool to confirm
Stop, breathe, and verify with a real person or trusted service first
Send half the amount to be safe
questions.right: Right. Never act on money instructions from a website or a tool. Check with a real person first, and if you suspect a scam, call the Canadian Anti-Fraud Centre at 1-888-495-8501.
questions.wrong: For anything involving money or bank details: stop, breathe, verify. Talk to a real person you trust first, and if you suspect a scam, call the Canadian Anti-Fraud Centre toll-free at 1-888-495-8501.

sections.heading: Your progress
sections.intro: Tick each item as you feel confident with it. This is saved on this device only, with no account needed.
items: I know a confident tone is not the same as a correct answer
I can say the three quiet questions: who is telling me this, how old is it, does a second place agree
I know where to look for the date and the author on a page
I have practised checking one question against two sources
I know to stop, breathe, and verify before acting on anything about money

success_state: Well done. You now have the whole habit: a confident tone is not proof, you ask who, how old, and whether a second source agrees, you check before you trust, and for anything about money you stop, breathe, and verify. That is real digital confidence, and you have earned it.
